"Venerable one, if a female trainee takes a precious object or something equivalent to a precious object, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a female novice or a male novice takes a precious object or something equivalent to a precious object, what is the consequence?"

"There is no offense."

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that bathing twice a month is a transgression except when the occasion for it has arisen. Venerable one, is there a case in which a monk may bathe constantly without incurring an offense?"

"Upāli, there is: bathing when any one of seven legitimate occasions has arisen."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives that the half-month has not yet elapsed when it actually has not elapsed, and bathes, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one perceives that the half-month has elapsed when it actually has not elapsed, and bathes, what is the consequence?"

"There is no offense."

"If one perceives that the half-month has not elapsed when it actually has elapsed, and bathes, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If one perceives that the half-month has elapsed when it actually has elapsed, and bathes, what is the consequence?"

"There is no offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives water as water and bathes in it, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"It is a wrong deed."

"If one perceives something that is not water as water and bathes in it, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If one perceives something that is not water as not water and bathes in it, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, is there a case in which a monk bathes at the proper time, with the blessing conferred, and yet incurs an offense?"

"Upāli, there is: one who, having sent away the bather, creeps in like a small bird."

"Venerable one, if a monk who has bathed within the half-month without having received the blessing has his sex changed and becomes a nun, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a nun who has bathed without having received the blessing has her sex changed and becomes a monk, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk bathes using something other than water, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, is there a case in which a monk may bathe constantly and yet not incur an offense?"

"Upāli, there is."

"Swimming across water, or bathing when rain falls." 

"Venerable one, if one who has received the precept bathes within the half-month without having received the blessing, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a nun bathes within the half-month without having received the blessing, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if female probationers (śikṣamāṇā), female novices, and male novices bathe within the half-month without having received the blessing, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that if a monk, while being solicited, causes another monk to feel regret, it is a transgression. If a monk causes a monk to feel regret by means of a message, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Likewise, if he causes regret through a letter, a gesture, through an intermediary, or passed from one to another — all of these are wrong deeds."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes a mad monk to feel regret, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Likewise, if he causes regret in a monk who is mentally disturbed, afflicted by illness, dull-witted, mute, deaf, asleep, with a speech impediment, intoxicated, in meditative absorption, or residing in another destination — all of these are wrong deeds."

In brief:
Voice, body, and solitude, mantra,
a sign, the fourth, the seventh,
householders and the like,
and the remainder — these apply to nuns.

"If one from the frontier causes regret in the noble language, and that monk does not understand the noble language, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If he perceives one who is fully ordained as not fully ordained, it is a wrong deed."

"If he perceives one who is not fully ordained as fully ordained and causes regret, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk intends to cause regret to one who is not fully ordained, perceiving him as not fully ordained, and it is accomplished, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If he intends it toward one who is not fully ordained, perceiving him as fully ordained, and it is accomplished, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If he intends it toward one who is not fully ordained, and it is accomplished with one who is fully ordained, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If he intends it toward one who is fully ordained, perceiving him as fully ordained, and it is accomplished, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If he intends it toward one who is fully ordained, and it is accomplished with one who has become fully ordained, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If he intends it toward one who is fully ordained, perceiving him as fully ordained, and it is accomplished with one who is fully ordained, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If he intends it toward one who is fully ordained, perceiving him as not fully ordained, and it is accomplished, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes regret to a layman, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

Likewise, causing regret to a woman, a paṇḍaka (a person of indeterminate sex), an expelled nun, one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has, with malicious intent, drawn blood from a Tathāgata, a tīrthika, one who has gone over to the tīrthikas, one abiding as a thief, one dwelling in isolation, one not dwelling in the community, one against whom an offense had previously arisen, and those who had previously been in conflict — causing regret to all of these constitutes a wrong deed in every case.

"Venerable one, if a monk causes regret to those who have caused a schism in the Saṅgha, to those who have sided with them, and to those who have administered a training rule — what is the consequence?"

"All of these are transgressions."

"Venerable one, is there a case where a monk causes regret to a monk and yet the offense of causing regret does not constitute a transgression?"

"Upāli, there is. If the offense in question is one accompanied by a residual factor, and he causes regret with respect to it."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes regret on behalf of others, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes regret to a nun, a probationer nun, a novice nun, or to the community of monks, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a nun causes regret to a nun, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If she causes regret to a monk, a probationer nun, a novice nun, or to male novices, all of these are wrong deeds."

Likewise, if a probationer nun, a novice nun, or male novices cause regret to one another, it is a wrong deed in every case.

"Venerable one, if one who administers a training rule causes regret to monks, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

In brief:
One who is mad, mentally disturbed,
one who is senseless, foolish, or asleep,
one who is delirious, one who is intoxicated,
one in meditative absorption — these last are the exceptions.

Then the venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that touching another with a finger is a transgression. If a monk touches a mad monk with a finger, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

Likewise, touching one who is mentally disturbed, foolish, mute, senseless, asleep, delirious, intoxicated, in meditative absorption, or a monk dwelling in another place — touching all of these is a wrong deed in every case.

In brief:
The body, a tooth, a fingernail,
hair, a covering, a wound — likewise —
laymen and others of that kind:
the marks, and then the fourth and the seventh.

"Venerable one, apart from touching with a finger, if a monk touches another using another part of the body — the head, the shoulder, the elbow, the knee, the heel — or using a stick, a stone, or a clod of earth — what is the consequence?"

"All of these are wrong deeds."

"Venerable one, if a monk whose bodily faculties are impaired touches one whose bodily faculties are not impaired, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk whose bodily faculties are not impaired touches one whose bodily faculties are impaired — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk touches using a tooth — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk touches using a fingernail — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk touches using a hair, or touches a hair — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk touches one who is covered — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk touches a wound, or touches at a wound — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk touches a layman — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

Likewise, if one touches in such a manner: a woman, a eunuch, a suspended nun, one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who with malicious intent has drawn blood from a Tathāgata, a non-Buddhist adherent (tīrthika), one who has gone over to the non-Buddhists, one who dwells among thieves, one dwelling apart, one who does not dwell in the community, one who has previously committed an offense, or one who has previously caused a schism — all of these are wrong deeds.

"Venerable one, if a monk touches one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, one who has taken sides in a schism, or one who has administered a training rule — what is the consequence?"

"All of these are transgressions."

"Venerable one, if a monk touches a fully ordained nun, or a nun in training, or a female novice, or male novices — what is the consequence?"

"All of these are wrong deeds."

"Venerable one, if a fully ordained nun touches a monk, a nun in training, a female novice, or male novices — what is the consequence?"

"All of these are wrong deeds."

"Venerable one, if a monk, while touching a monk, has a sex change and becomes a nun — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a fully ordained nun, while touching a nun, has a sex change and becomes a monk — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a fully ordained person as fully ordained and touches that person — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one perceives a fully ordained person as not fully ordained and touches that person — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If one perceives a person who is not fully ordained as fully ordained and touches that person — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If one perceives a person who is not fully ordained as not fully ordained and touches that person — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

Likewise, the fourfold matrix is to be applied also to the case of perceiving a human being as a human being.

"Venerable one, if one intends to touch a person who is not fully ordained and touches one who is not fully ordained — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If one intends to touch a person who is not fully ordained and touches one who is in the course of receiving full ordination — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If one intends to touch a person who is not fully ordained and touches one who is fully ordained — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If one intends to touch one who is in the course of receiving full ordination and touches one who is in the course of receiving full ordination — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If one intends to touch one who is in the course of receiving full ordination and touches one who is fully ordained — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If one intends to touch one who is fully ordained and touches one who is fully ordained — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one intends to touch one who is fully ordained and touches one who is not fully ordained — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if one who has administered a training rule touches a monk — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a fully ordained nun touches a fully ordained nun — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"With regard to a nun in training, a female novice, and male novices — it is a wrong deed."

In brief:
A message, a letter, a hand-signal,
speaking through another, and from one to another —
a mad person, one whose mind is disturbed, one who is ill,

one who is deaf-mute, one who is simple-minded, one who is asleep,
one who is vomiting, one who is intoxicated,
one who has entered meditative absorption, and one traveling elsewhere — these are the last.

Venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if one causes satisfaction with water it becomes a transgression. Venerable one, if a monk causes satisfaction with water by means of a message — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Likewise, if one causes satisfaction with water by means of a letter, a hand-signal, speaking through another, or passing the message from one to another — all of these become wrong deeds."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes satisfaction to a mad woman with water — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Likewise, if one causes satisfaction to one whose mind is disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is simple-minded, one who is mute, one who is deaf-mute, one who is asleep, one who is vomiting, one who is intoxicated, one who has entered meditative absorption, or one who is dwelling elsewhere — all of these become wrong deeds."

Just as the manner in which one causes satisfaction is elaborated, so too playing, expression of desire, laughing, running, and physical striking are to be set forth in full.

In brief:
Water, two, and likewise mantra,
another through another's characteristics,
seclusion, the fourth, a hermaphrodite,
one who has administered a training rule, and a fully ordained nun.

"Venerable one, if a monk causes satisfaction by means of something other than water — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes satisfaction with drops of falling rain, or with drops of snow, or with drops of dew — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk renders himself invisible by means of mantra or medicine and then causes satisfaction — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes another monk to bring about satisfaction — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes satisfaction on behalf of others — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if while a monk is causing satisfaction with water his characteristics change and he becomes a fully ordained nun — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if while a fully ordained nun is causing satisfaction with water her characteristics change and she becomes a fully ordained monk — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a secluded place as not secluded and causes satisfaction — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If he perceives water as not water, it becomes a wrong deed."

"If he perceives what is not water as not water and causes satisfaction — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Likewise, if one perceives a human as a human, this too is to be applied in four ways."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes a hermaphrodite to experience satisfaction — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Likewise, if one causes a female hermaphrodite or a person of dual characteristics to experience satisfaction, all of these become wrong deeds."

Just as the manner of causing satisfaction is elaborated, so too playing, desire, laughing, running, and physical striking are likewise to be set forth in full.

"Venerable one, if one who has administered a training rule causes satisfaction — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a fully ordained nun causes satisfaction with water or causes another to do so — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

With regard to a nun in training, a female novice, and male novices — it is a wrong deed.

In brief:
A mad person, one whose mind is disturbed,
a female hermaphrodite, one traveling in an emanated form,
space, mantra, characteristics,
the fourth — and likewise a hermaphrodite.

Venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk sleeps together with a woman in the same dwelling it becomes a transgression. Venerable one, if a monk sleeps together with a mad woman in the same dwelling — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Likewise, if one sleeps together with one whose mind is disturbed, one afflicted by illness, or one dwelling elsewhere, in the same dwelling — it is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk sleeps together with an emanated woman in the same dwelling — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk sleeps together with a woman in the same dwelling, up in the open sky — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk renders himself invisible by means of mantra or medicine and sleeps together with a woman in the same dwelling — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk is sleeping together with a woman in the same dwelling and his sex changes so that he becomes a nun — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a nun is sleeping together with a man in the same dwelling and her sex changes so that she becomes a monk — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a woman as a woman and sleeps with her — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If he perceives a woman as not a woman — there is no offense."

"If he perceives a non-woman as a woman — it is a wrong deed."

"If he perceives a non-woman as a non-woman — there is no offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a human woman as human and sleeps together with her in the same dwelling — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If he perceives a human as non-human — it is a wrong deed."

"If he perceives a non-human as human — it is a wrong deed."

"If he perceives a non-human as non-human — it is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk sleeps together with a hermaphrodite in the same dwelling — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

In summary:

A mountain ravine, dense forest,
Surrounded, covered, a large one,
Grasped, likewise by day,
Giving the training, and a nun.

"Venerable one, if a monk sleeps together with a woman in a mountain ravine, a dense forest, or the hollow of a tree — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk sleeps together with a woman wholly covered, or half-encircled, or not encircled — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk sleeps together with a woman encircled by a boundary, uncovered, half-covered, or half-uncovered — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if one sleeps in the same dwelling as a being born in an animal rebirth it is a wrong deed. Of what kind is that?"

"Upāli, it is a great female animal."

"Of what kind, great one?"

He declared: "Among birds — a hen, or another like a hen. Among four-footed animals — a female monkey, or another like a female monkey."

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk sleeps in the same dwelling together with a non-human woman it is a wrong deed. Of what kind is a non-human?"

"One who possesses and displays all her limbs."

"Venerable one, if a monk sleeps together with a woman in the same dwelling during the daytime — what is the consequence?"

"Upāli, up until dawn it is a wrong deed. From dawn onward it becomes a transgression."

"Venerable one, if one who has been given the training sleeps together with a woman in the same dwelling — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a nun sleeps together with a man in the same dwelling — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

For a female probationer, a novice nun, and male novices — it is a wrong deed.

In summary:

Sending a message, a letter, a hand-signal,
Another saying it, from one to another,
Mad, mentally disturbed, ill,
Mute, foolish, asleep,
Delirious, intoxicated,
In meditative absorption, and finally the one departing.

Thus did the venerable Upāli petition the Blessed One, the Buddha.

"Venerable one, if the Blessed One has declared that blaming or causing to be blamed incurs a transgression — then, venerable one, if a monk causes a monk to be blamed by means of a messenger, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Likewise, if it is done through a letter, a hand-signal, through another person speaking, or passed along from one to another causing blame — all of these are wrong deeds."

"Likewise, if a monk who is mentally disturbed, afflicted by illness, foolish, mute, deaf, asleep, delirious, intoxicated, in meditative absorption, or one who has gone to dwell elsewhere — if such a one causes blame or is caused to blame another — all of these are wrong deeds."

In summary:

By voice, by body, and by a secluded place's signal,
Another blamed by another's seventh,
Laymen and the rest,
The fourth case — including the night — is likewise.

"Venerable one, if a noble monk causes a monk to be blamed in the noble language, and that monk does not know the noble language — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If a noble monk causes a monk to be blamed in a frontier language, and that monk does not know the frontier language — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If a frontier monk causes a monk to be blamed in a frontier language, and that monk does not know the frontier language — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If a frontier monk causes a monk to be blamed in the noble language, and that monk does not know the noble language — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk blames a monk using a physical gesture — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving a secluded place as non-secluded, blames a monk — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk renders himself invisible by means of a mantra or a drug and then blames a monk — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes another to be blamed — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk blames a monk on behalf of another monk — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if the blame was prepared before full ordination and completed before full ordination — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If it was prepared before full ordination and completed during the act of full ordination — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If it was prepared before full ordination and completed after full ordination — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If it was prepared during the act of full ordination and completed during the act of full ordination — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If it was prepared during the act of full ordination and completed after full ordination — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If it was prepared after full ordination and completed after full ordination — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If it was prepared after full ordination and completed before full ordination — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk blames a layman — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Likewise, if it concerns a eunuch, an expelled nun, one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who with malicious intent has drawn the blood of a Tathāgata, a non-Buddhist adherent, one who has gone over to the non-Buddhists, one who dwells among thieves, one who dwells apart, one who does not dwell in the community, one against whom an earlier offence has occurred, or one against whom there was a prior dispute — if blame is given or caused to be given to any of these, all such acts are wrong deeds."

"Venerable one, if a monk directly blames or causes to be blamed a monk who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, one who has sided with the schismatic faction, or a monk who has been given a formal instruction — what is the consequence?"

"All of these are transgressions."

"Venerable one, if a monk directly causes a monk to blame a layman — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Likewise, a eunuch, an expelled nun, one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, and one who with malicious intent has drawn the blood of a Tathāgata —"

one who holds non-Buddhist views, one who has gone over to non-Buddhist views, one who is dwelling illicitly, one who is living separately, one who is not residing in the community, one against whom a prior offense has arisen, one who was previously involved in a dispute, one who has sided with a faction, a monk who has been given a formal instruction, a nun, a female probationer, a female novice, or male novices — if a monk directly blames or causes any of these to be blamed, all of these are transgressions.

"Venerable one, if a monk directly blames or causes to be blamed a nun, a female probationer, a female novice, or male novices — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a nun directly blames or causes to be blamed a monk, a female probationer, a female novice, or male novices — what is the consequence?"

"All of these are transgressions."

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving one who is fully ordained as fully ordained, directly blames or causes him to be blamed — what is the consequence?"

"It is a downfall."

"If he perceives one who is fully ordained as not fully ordained, it is a transgression. If he perceives one who is not fully ordained as fully ordained, it is a transgression. If he perceives one who is not fully ordained as not fully ordained and directly blames or causes him to be blamed, it is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk directly blames or causes a monk to be blamed and, while this is occurring, that monk changes his status and becomes a nun — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a nun directly blames or causes a nun to be blamed and, while this is occurring, that nun changes her status and becomes a monk — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if one who has been given a formal instruction directly blames or causes a monk to be blamed — what is the consequence?"

"It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a nun directly blames or causes a nun to be blamed — what is the consequence?"

"It is a downfall."

As for a female probationer, a female novice, and male novices, these are to be explained extensively as transgressions.

In brief:

By messenger, by letter, by hand-signal,
through another's words, and from one to another;
one who is mad, mentally disturbed, or ill,
one who is mute, simpleminded, or asleep,
one who is intoxicated, one who is drunk,
one in meditative absorption, and one who has gone elsewhere — these are the last.

The venerable Upāli then asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk conceals or causes to be concealed the alms bowl, the robe, or any other requisite of an ascetic belonging to another monk, it is a downfall. Venerable one, if a monk causes such concealment by means of a messenger — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Likewise, if it is done by letter, by hand-signal, through another's words, or by passing it from one to another and causing the concealment — all of these are transgressions."

"Venerable one, if a monk conceals or causes to be concealed the alms bowl, the robe, or any other requisite of an ascetic belonging to a monk who is mad — what is the consequence?"

"All of these are transgressions."

"Likewise, if it involves the alms bowl, the robe, or any other requisite of an ascetic belonging to a monk who is mentally disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is simpleminded, one who is mute, one who is blind, one who is asleep, one who is intoxicated, one who is drunk, one who is in meditative absorption, or one who has gone to dwell elsewhere — if anyone conceals or causes the concealment of such items, all of these are transgressions."

In brief:

Unsuitable items and likewise mantras,
small and large, and also robes;
laypeople and so forth;
with marks, and the fourth, and the seventh;
one Saṅgha acting on behalf of another Saṅgha,
giving a training precept, and a nun.

"Venerable one, if a monk conceals or causes to be concealed the alms bowl, the robe, or any other requisite of an ascetic belonging to another monk by hiding something that is unsuitable — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk, by means of a mantra or medicine, renders a monk invisible and conceals his alms bowl —"

"— or a robe, or any other requisite of an ascetic, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk by means of a mantra, or medicine, or supernatural power conceals a monk's alms bowl, or robe, or any other requisite of an ascetic — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes to be concealed a robe smaller than a cubit, or a small alms bowl, or an alms bowl larger than the standard measure — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk conceals or causes to be concealed, not the alms bowl, or robe, or any other requisite of a monk proper, but rather some other item belonging to a layperson — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes to be concealed a layperson's vessel, or robe, or any other such item — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

Likewise in all the following cases: one who has eaten a meal with a hermaphrodite; one who has expelled a nun; one who has killed his father; one who has killed his mother; one who has killed an arhat; one who has drawn blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent; a tīrthika; one who has gone over to the tīrthikas; one who is a thief living among the community; one who is living separately; one who is not residing properly; one who was previously involved in a schism; one who has previously incurred an offense — if the alms bowl, or robe, or any other requisite of an ascetic belonging to such a person is concealed or caused to be concealed, all cases constitute a transgression.

"Venerable one, if a monk conceals or causes to be concealed the alms bowl or robe of a monk who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, or who has taken sides in a schism, or who has received a training precept — what is the consequence?"
"All are downfalls."

"Venerable one, if a monk conceals or causes to be concealed the alms bowl, or robe, or any other requisite of an ascetic belonging to a nun, a female probationer, a female novice, or a male novice — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a nun conceals or causes to be concealed the alms bowl, or robe, or any other requisite of an ascetic belonging to a monk, a female probationer, a female novice, or a male novice — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes a layperson to conceal in plain sight a monk's alms bowl, or robe, or any other requisite of a monk — what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

Likewise, in all the following cases: one who has eaten a meal with a hermaphrodite; one who has expelled a nun; one who has killed his father; one who has killed his mother; one who has killed an arhat; one who has drawn blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent; a tīrthika; one who has gone over to the tīrthikas; one who is a thief living among the community; one who is living separately; one who is not residing properly; one who has previously incurred an offense; one who was previously involved in a schism; one who has taken sides in a schism; one who has received a training precept — and likewise a monk, a nun, a female probationer, a female novice, or a male novice — if any of them are caused to conceal such requisites in plain sight, it is a downfall.

"Venerable one, if a monk conceals or causes to be concealed the alms bowl, or robe, or any other requisite of an ascetic belonging to a monk, and in the meantime that monk changes his status and becomes a nun — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a nun conceals or causes to be concealed the alms bowl, or robe, or any other requisite of an ascetic belonging to a nun, and in the meantime that nun changes her status and becomes a monk — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk conceals — perceiving a fully ordained person as fully ordained — what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"If he perceives a fully ordained person as not fully ordained, it is a transgression. If he perceives one who is not fully ordained as fully ordained, it is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if one who is not fully ordained is concealed while being perceived as not fully ordained — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if one sets out to conceal while the other is not fully ordained, and the concealment is accomplished while the other is still not fully ordained — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one sets out to conceal while the other is not fully ordained, and the concealment is accomplished just as the other becomes fully ordained — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If one sets out to conceal while the other is not fully ordained, and the concealment is accomplished after the other has been fully ordained — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If one sets out to conceal just as the other is becoming fully ordained, and the concealment is accomplished just as the other is becoming fully ordained — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If one sets out to conceal just as the other is becoming fully ordained, and the concealment is accomplished after the other has been fully ordained — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If one sets out to conceal while the other is fully ordained, and the concealment is accomplished after the other has been fully ordained — what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"If one sets out to conceal while the other is fully ordained, and the concealment is accomplished while the other is not fully ordained — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives another person the bowl or robe of a monk, or any other requisite of a renunciant, to be hidden — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk hides the property of the Saṅgha, or gives it to another to be hidden — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk hides the bowl or robe of a monk, or any other requisite for the livelihood of a renunciant, on behalf of another — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if one who gives the training hides or gives to another to be hidden the bowl or robe of a monk, or any other requisite of a renunciant — what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a nun hides or gives to another to be hidden the bowl or robe of a nun, or any other requisite of a renunciant — what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

For novice nuns, novice nuns, and male novices it is a transgression.

In summary, the categories are:
by messenger, written message, gesture,
through another's word, or passed from one to the next,
in the case of one who is mad, mentally disturbed, or ill,
a mute, a deaf person, one who is asleep,
one who has lockjaw, one who is intoxicated,
one who has entered absorption, or one dwelling elsewhere — these are the last.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has taught that if a monk gives a robe and it is used without being reclaimed, it becomes a downfall. If a monk gives a robe to a monk by messenger and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Likewise, if a robe given by written message, gesture, through another's word, or passed from one to the next is used without being returned — all of these are transgressions."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe to a mad monk and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

Likewise, if a robe is given to a monk who is mentally disturbed, afflicted by illness, confused, mute, deaf, asleep, suffering from lockjaw, intoxicated, in meditative absorption, or dwelling in another place, and it is used without being returned — all of these are transgressions.

In summary:
improper cloth, and likewise mantras,
small and large robes,
householders and the like,
by night, and the fourth, and the seventh,
another's property and given to another,
given as training, and a nun.

"Venerable one, is there any case in which a monk gives a robe to a monk, and even though it is used without being reclaimed, the offense does not become a downfall?"
"Upāli, there is. It is when the cloth has become improper. Improper cloth is: wool from a female yak, wool from an ox, wool from a deer, wool from a goat, mixed wool, or wool that has not been woven. If a robe of such material is given and used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives something produced by mantra, medicine, or miraculous transformation, and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe that is smaller than a cubit in measure, or of the size of a robe of the Sugata (the Well-Gone One, an epithet of the Buddha), and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives items of a recluse's requisites other than robes, and they are used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe to a layman, and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe to a female monk who eats together with the community, or to a hermaphrodite, and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

Likewise, if a robe is given to one who has killed a father, or a mother, or an arhat; to one who has drawn blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent; to a non-Buddhist adherent; to one who has gone over to non-Buddhist adherents; to one who is in hiding; to one who does not remain in the community; to one who dwells in seclusion; to one against whom a prior offence has arisen; or to one who was previously in dispute — and in each case it is used without being reclaimed — all such cases are transgressions.

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe to a monk who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, or to one who sides with such a person, or to a monk who confers the training precepts, and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe to a nun, a probationary nun, a female novice, or a male novice, and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe to a nun, a probationary nun, a female novice, or a male novice, and while it is being used without being reclaimed, a change of status occurs and the recipient becomes a fully ordained nun — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe to a monk, and while it is being used without being reclaimed, a change of status occurs and the recipient becomes a fully ordained nun — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a fully ordained nun gives a robe to a fully ordained nun, and while it is being used without being reclaimed, a change of status occurs and the recipient becomes a fully ordained monk — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe to one who has received full ordination, perceiving that person as fully ordained, and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"If one perceives a fully ordained person as not fully ordained — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If one perceives a person who has not received full ordination as fully ordained — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If one perceives a person who has not received full ordination as not fully ordained, gives a robe, and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if while one has not yet received full ordination a robe is given, and before full ordination has been received it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If it is given before full ordination, and is used without being reclaimed while full ordination is in the process of being conferred — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If it is given before full ordination, and is used without being reclaimed after full ordination has been completed — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If a robe is given while full ordination is in the process of being conferred, and it is used without being reclaimed while full ordination is still in the process of being conferred — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If a robe is given while full ordination is in the process of being conferred, and it is used without being reclaimed after full ordination has been completed — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If a robe is given after full ordination has been completed, and it is used without being reclaimed after full ordination has been completed — what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"If a robe is given after full ordination has been completed, and it is used without being reclaimed before full ordination was completed — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe away that he received from another monk, and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a monk a robe that is held in common, and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a monk a robe on another's behalf, and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if one who confers the training precepts gives a robe to a monk and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

For a probationary nun, a female novice, and male novices, all such cases are to be stated as transgressions.

As for giving the surplus property of the Saṅgha with malicious intent — the distinctions are to be set forth in the same manner as what has been described regarding malicious intent toward a root downfall.

The Noble Vinaya Text, the Thirteenth Fascicle.

In brief:
One who is insane, one whose mind is disturbed,
One who is ill, and likewise one who uses mantra,
The sky, the fourth case with its counterpart,
Youths and those of indeterminate sex,
And likewise an emanated being of indeterminate sex.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that any monk who, without a man present, enters into a secluded place together with a woman — that is a transgression. Venerable one, if a monk enters into a secluded place together with a woman who is insane — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."
"And likewise with a woman whose mind is disturbed, a woman afflicted by illness, a foolish woman, a mute woman, a deaf woman, and a woman who is dwelling elsewhere but is traveling on the road together with him — all such cases are transgressions."

"Venerable one, if a monk enters into a secluded place together with an insane man and a woman — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."
"And likewise with a man whose mind is disturbed, a man afflicted by illness, a foolish man, a mute man, a deaf man, and a man dwelling elsewhere — if he enters the secluded place together with such a man and also with a woman, all such cases are transgressions."

"If a monk enters into a secluded place together with a woman and a person of indeterminate sex — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk makes himself invisible through mantra or medicine and then, without a man present, enters into a secluded place together with a woman — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk, without a man present, travels through the sky together with a woman — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk who has entered into a secluded place together with a woman, without a man present, then undergoes a change of sex-mark and becomes a nun — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a nun who has entered into a secluded place together with a man then undergoes a change of sex-mark and becomes a monk — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving a human woman as a human, enters into a secluded place with her — what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."
"If he perceives a human as not human — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."
"If he perceives a non-human as human — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."
"If he perceives a non-human as non-human — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving a human woman as a woman, enters into a secluded place with her — what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."
"If he perceives a human woman as a man and enters into a secluded place — what is the consequence?"
"There is no offence."
"If he perceives a man as a woman and enters into a secluded place — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."
"If he perceives a man as a man and enters into a secluded place — what is the consequence?"
"There is no offence."

"Venerable one, if a monk enters into a secluded place together with a young woman, without a man present — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk enters into a secluded place together with a person of indeterminate sex — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk, without a man present, enters into a secluded place together with a woman — what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a monk enters into a secluded place together with a person of indeterminate sex — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if one who confers training precepts enters into a secluded place together with a woman, without a man present — what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a nun, without a woman present, enters into a secluded place together with a man — what is the consequence?"
"It is as the matter stands."

For a probationary nun, a female novice, and male novices, all such cases are to be stated as transgressions.

In brief:
One who has become insane, one whose mind is disturbed,
One who is ill, one who is deaf, one who is a traveler —
The sky, the sex-change case, the fourth case,
An emanated being, and the path of one of indeterminate sex.

the wrong path, and the case of the nun.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk travels along a road together with a large band of thieves, it is a downfall. Venerable one, if a monk travels along a road together with a single thief who is insane, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Likewise, if he travels along a road together with a large band of thieves who are mentally disturbed, who are tormented by illness, who are foolish, who are mute, who are deaf, or who are staying in another destination — in all such cases, what is the consequence?"
"In all such cases it is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk, having made himself invisible by means of a mantra or a medicine, travels in the company of a large band of thieves, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk travels through the sky together with a large band of thieves, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk is traveling together with a large band of thieves and along the way his sex changes and he becomes a nun, what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a nun is traveling along a road together with a large band of thieves and along the way her sex changes and she becomes a monk, what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a large band of thieves as a large band of thieves and then travels along a road with them, what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"If he perceives a large band of thieves as not a large band of thieves and travels with them, what is the consequence?"
"There is no offense."

"If he perceives those who are not a large band of thieves as a large band of thieves and travels with them, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If he perceives those who are not a large band of thieves as not a large band of thieves, what is the consequence?"
"There is no offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a person as a person and then travels along a road together with a large band of thieves, what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"If he perceives a person as not a person, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If he perceives one who is not a person as a person, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If he perceives one who is not a person as not a person, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk travels along a road together with an emanated likeness of a large band of thieves, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk travels along a road together with a thief who is a person of indeterminate sex, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, are there cases in which a monk travels along a road together with a large band of thieves and yet incurs no offense?"
"Upāli, there are. If within the distance of one league he turns back, or if the thieves seize the monk and lead him away, or if they themselves disperse, or if he loses the road and someone shows him the way."

"Venerable one, if a monk travels along a road that is not the same road as that taken by a large band of thieves, what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if one who has been given a training rule travels along a road together with a large band of thieves, what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a nun travels along a road together with a large band of thieves, what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

For a probationary nun, a female novice, and male novices, it is a transgression.

In brief:
The prior disturbance, full ordination, and the sex-change case,
The fourth: one insane, one mentally disturbed,
One ill, one deaf, one who is traveling,
A layman and so forth, a laywoman,
One given a training rule, and a nun.

The venerable Upāli then asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk confers full ordination as a monk upon a person who has not yet reached the age of twenty, it is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a monk confers full ordination upon a person who has not yet reached the age of twenty, perceiving them to be of that age, does that constitute a valid full ordination?"

"Upāli, these four are prior disturbances. The first: the candidate has not yet reached the age of twenty, the monk perceives them as not having reached twenty, and when the monk asks whether they have reached the age of twenty, the candidate says, 'I know and am aware that I have not reached twenty — I have no doubt about this.' If that person is then given full ordination as a monk by the monk, this is the first prior disturbance. The second: the candidate has not yet reached the age of twenty, the monk perceives them as not having reached twenty, and when the monk asks whether they have reached twenty, the candidate says, 'I do not know, I do not recall.' If that person is then given full ordination as a monk by the monks, this is the second prior disturbance. The third: the candidate has not yet reached the age of twenty, the monk perceives them as not having reached twenty, and when the monk asks whether they have reached twenty, the candidate says, 'I am uncertain.' If that person is then given full ordination as a monk by the monk, this is the third prior disturbance. The fourth: the candidate has not yet reached the age of twenty, the monk perceives them as not having reached twenty, and when the monk asks the question, the candidate gives no answer. If that person is then given full ordination as a monk by the monks, this is the fourth prior disturbance. Upāli, apart from these four prior disturbances, all remaining cases constitute a valid full ordination."

"Venerable one, if a monk confers full ordination as a monk upon a person who has not yet reached the age of twenty, and that person then undergoes a sex change and becomes a nun, what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a nun confers full ordination as a nun upon someone who has not yet reached the age of twenty, or who has not yet reached the age of twelve, and that person undergoes a sex change and becomes a monk, what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving someone who has not yet reached the age of twenty as not having reached that age, confers full ordination upon them, what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"If one has not yet reached the age of twenty but is perceived as having done so, and full ordination is conferred, there is no fault."

"If one has reached the age of twenty but is perceived as not having done so, and full ordination is conferred, it becomes a wrongdoing."

"If one has reached the age of twenty and is perceived as having done so, and full ordination is conferred, there is no fault."

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving an insane person as not having reached the age of twenty, confers full ordination, what is the consequence?"
"It is a wrongdoing."

Likewise, if one perceives a mentally disturbed person, one afflicted by illness, a simpleton, a mute, a deaf person, or one who is traveling elsewhere as not having reached the age of twenty and confers full ordination upon any of them, in every case it becomes a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving a layman as not having reached the age of twenty, confers full ordination, what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

A male novice is likewise the same.

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving a sexually indeterminate person as not having reached the age of twenty, confers full ordination, what is the consequence?"
"It is a wrongdoing."

Likewise, if one perceives as not having reached twenty any of the following and confers full ordination upon them: a nun who has been expelled, one who has killed their father, one who has killed their mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has maliciously drawn blood from a Tathāgata, a tīrthika, one who has gone over to the tīrthikas, one who is a thief by position, one who is not a resident, one who is dwelling separately, one in whom a prior disturbance has occurred, or one in whom a prior fault has arisen — in every case it becomes a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, can it occur that a monk confers full ordination perceiving the candidate as not having reached the age of twenty, yet it neither constitutes a fault nor a downfall, and the full ordination is properly conferred?"
"Upāli, it can."

"Go to a person who has not yet reached the age of twenty and confer full ordination upon them."
"Venerable one, if one confers full ordination by means of giving the training upon a person who has not yet reached the age of twenty, what does that become?"
"It becomes a downfall."
"Venerable one, if a nun confers full ordination upon a young woman who has not yet reached the age of twenty, or upon a married woman who has not yet reached the age of twelve, what does that become?"
"It becomes a downfall. For a female probationer, a female novice, and male novices, there is no fault."

In brief:
By messenger, letter, gesture,
through another's word, or passing it from one to another,
while insane, while mentally disturbed,
while ill, while mute, or while traveling — these are the categories.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk digs the earth or has it dug with his own hand, it becomes a downfall. Venerable one, if a monk has earth dug by means of a messenger, what does that become?"
"It becomes a wrongdoing."
"Likewise, if one causes earth to be dug by means of a letter, by a gesture, through another's word, or relayed from one to another — all of these become wrongdoings."
"Venerable one, if a monk has a madman dig the earth, what does that become?"
"It becomes a wrongdoing. Likewise, having one who is mentally disturbed, afflicted by illness, dull-witted, mute, incapable of speech, or residing in another place dig the earth — all of these become wrongdoings."

In brief:
At dawn, on the fourth and seventh,
in the presence of householders and others,
without sound, without body, without intervention,
a stake, a clod, the burning of earth.

"Venerable one, if a monk, while digging the earth with his own hand, undergoes a change of sex and becomes a nun, what does that become?"
"It becomes a downfall."
"Venerable one, if a nun, while digging the earth with her own hand, undergoes a change of sex and becomes a monk, what does that become?"
"It becomes a downfall."
"Venerable one, if a monk perceives earth to be earth and digs it or has it dug, what does that become?"
"It becomes a downfall."
"If he perceives earth as not being earth, there is no fault."
"If he causes what is not earth to be dug while perceiving it as earth, it becomes a wrongdoing."
"If he perceives what is not earth as not being earth, there is no fault."
"Venerable one, if a monk causes another to dig the earth, what does that become?"
"It becomes a wrongdoing."
"Venerable one, if a monk digs for the sake of another, what does that become?"
"It becomes a downfall."
"Venerable one, if one prepares to dig before full ordination and completes it before full ordination, what does that become?"
"It becomes a wrongdoing."
"If one prepares before full ordination and completes it at the moment of full ordination, what does that become?"
"It becomes a wrongdoing."
"If one prepares before full ordination and completes it after full ordination, what does that become?"
"It becomes a wrongdoing."
"If one prepares at the moment of full ordination and completes it at the moment of full ordination, what does that become?"
"It becomes a wrongdoing."
"If one prepares at the moment of full ordination and completes it after full ordination, what does that become?"
"It becomes a wrongdoing."
"If one prepares after full ordination and completes it after full ordination, what does that become?"
"It becomes a downfall."
"If one prepares after full ordination and completes it before full ordination, what does that become?"
"It becomes a wrongdoing."
"Venerable one, if a monk directly causes a householder to dig the earth, what does that become?"
"It becomes a downfall."
Likewise for a woman, a hermaphrodite, an expelled nun, one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, one who has maliciously drawn blood from a Tathāgata, a tīrthika, one who has gone over to the tīrthikas, a thief by position, one who is dwelling separately, one who is not a resident, one in whom a prior disturbance has occurred, one in whom a prior fault has arisen, one who has drawn near to disrobing, one who has given back the training, a monk, a nun, a female probationer, a female novice, and male novices — if he directly causes any of them to dig the earth, all of these become downfalls.

Venerable ones, if a noble monk invites someone to dig earth using the noble language, and that person does not seek permission in the noble language, what does this become? It is a misdeed. If a noble one invites someone to dig earth using the border language, and that person does not seek permission in the border language, what does this become? It is a misdeed. Venerable ones, if a border monk invites someone to dig earth using the border language, and that person does not seek permission in the border language, what does this become? It is a misdeed. If a border person invites someone to dig earth using the noble language, and that person does not seek permission in the noble language, what does this become? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, if a monk causes earth to be dug by means of a bodily gesture, what does this become? It is a misdeed. Venerable ones, if a monk causes unsettled earth to be dug, what does this become? It is a misdeed. Venerable ones, if a monk drives a peg into the earth, what does this become? It is a downfall. Venerable ones, if he then pulls it out, what does this become? It is a misdeed. Venerable ones, if a monk scrapes mud from the earth, what does this become? It is a misdeed. Venerable ones, if a monk presses down on the earth, what does this become? It is a misdeed. Venerable ones, if a monk digs earth that contains ox dung or has become sodden and clumped, what does this become? It is a misdeed. Venerable ones, if a monk digs burnt earth, what does this become? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, if one who has given the training digs or causes the digging of earth with his own fingernail, what does this become? It is a downfall. Venerable ones, if a nun digs or causes the digging of earth with her own fingernail, what does this become? It is a downfall. For a female probationer it is a misdeed. For a female novice and a male novice there is no fault.

In brief:

By message, by letter, by hand signal,
by word of another, relayed from one to the next,
by one who is mad, whose mind is disturbed, who is ill,
by one who is mute, who is foolish, who is asleep,
by one who is stammering, who is intoxicated,
and one who is in meditative absorption — these are the last.

Then the venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: Venerable Blessed One, you have declared that a monk should accept an invitation within four months, and that accepting beyond that becomes a downfall. Venerable one, if a monk, for however long and for however many times he has been invited, accepts and seeks food beyond that limit by means of a message, what does this become? It is a misdeed. Likewise, if he accepts and eats beyond that limit by means of a letter, a hand signal, the word of another, or by relay from one to the next, all of these become misdeeds.

Venerable ones, if a monk is invited by a madman, and he accepts and seeks food beyond that limit, what does this become? It is a misdeed. Likewise, if one whose mind is disturbed, one who is afflicted by illness, one who is foolish, one who is mute, one who is deaf, one who is asleep, one who is stammering, one who is intoxicated, one who is in meditative absorption, or one who is dwelling elsewhere — if any of these invite for however long, and the monk accepts and eats beyond that limit, all of these become misdeeds.

In brief:

What is unsuitable and what is excluded,
what pertains to the name, and likewise the fourth —
what is appointed, and again the interruption,
and another's on behalf of another — these are the seventh.

Venerable ones, if a monk is invited for however long and for however much food and drink, and he accepts food and drink that is suitable beyond that limit, what does this become? It is a downfall. Venerable ones, if a monk is invited for however long and however much food and drink, and setting aside that food and drink, he seeks other things — medicines — intending to use them as medicine, and accepts and receives those things that are not food, what does this become? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, if a monk is invited for however long and for however much, and while accepting beyond that limit his status changes and he becomes a nun, what does this become? It is a downfall. Venerable ones, if a nun is invited for however long and for however much, and while accepting beyond that limit her status changes and she becomes a monk, what does this become? It is a downfall.

Venerable ones, if a monk, perceiving a human being as a human being, solicits and accepts from him, what does this become? It is a downfall. If he perceives a human being as a non-human, it becomes a misdeed. If he perceives a non-human as a human being, it becomes a misdeed. If he perceives a non-human as a non-human and accepts beyond that limit and receives, what does this become? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, is there any case in which a monk, however long and for however much he has been invited, accepts within that limit and yet incurs no offense? Upāli, there is. It is as a monk hears when invited to a village where the training precepts are given. Venerable ones, is there any case in which a monk, however long and for however much he has been invited, accepts beyond that limit and yet incurs no offense? Upāli, there is. It is when that monk, while still there, flees and goes elsewhere, and any one of the eight interruptions arises.

Venerable ones, if a monk, invited for however long and for however much, accepts beyond that limit on behalf of another and receives, what does this become? It is a misdeed. Venerable ones, if a monk, invited for however long, accepts beyond that limit and gives the invitation to another who then receives, what does this become? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, if one who has not received full ordination accepts, and one who has not received full ordination receives, what does this become? It is a misdeed. If one who has not received full ordination accepts, and one who is in the act of receiving full ordination receives, what does this become? It is a misdeed. If one who has not received full ordination accepts, and one who has fully received ordination receives, what does this become? It is a misdeed. If one who is in the act of receiving full ordination accepts, and one who is in the act of receiving full ordination receives, what does this become? It is a misdeed. If one who is in the act of receiving full ordination accepts, and one who has fully received ordination receives, what does this become? It is a misdeed. If one who has fully received ordination accepts, and one who has fully received ordination receives, what does this become? It is a downfall. If one who has fully received ordination accepts, and one who has not received full ordination receives, what does this become? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, if one accepts more than what the training precepts allow and then receives, what does this become? It is a downfall. Venerable ones, if a nun accepts more than that limit and receives, what does this become? It is a downfall. If a female trainee (śikṣamāṇā), a novice nun, or male novices accept more than that limit and receive, what does this become? It is a misdeed.

In brief:
Through messenger, letter, gesture,
through the word of another, through relay from one to the next,
through one who is mad, mentally disturbed, or ill,
through one who is deaf, dull-witted, asleep,
through one with cleft palate, one who is intoxicated,
and one entering meditative absorption — these are the final cases.

Then the venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: Venerable one, the Blessed One has also declared that if a monk is instructed by another monk — "Venerable one, train in this precept" — and that monk says, "I will not train in this precept as the venerable one has instructed me," this becomes a downfall. Venerable one, if a monk instructs another monk, and through a messenger that monk says, "I will not train in this precept as the venerable ones have instructed me," what does this become? It is a misdeed. Likewise, if he says so through a letter, through a gesture, through the word of another, or through relay from one to the next — all of these become misdeeds.

Venerable ones, if the monks instruct a monk and a mad monk says, "I will not train in this precept as the venerable ones have instructed me," what does this become? It is a misdeed. Likewise, one who is mentally disturbed, one tormented by illness, one who is dull-witted, one who is mute, one who is deaf, one who is asleep, one with a cleft palate,

one who is intoxicated, one in meditative absorption, and monks dwelling in another region — if any of these say, "I will not train in this precept as the venerable ones have instructed me," all of these become misdeeds.

In brief:

By voice, by body, by solitude,
by a seventh party acting for another,
by laypeople and the like —
these are the mark: the fourth and the seventh.

Venerable ones, if a monk instructs a monk in the noble language saying, "I will not train in this precept as the venerable one has instructed me," and that monk does not understand the noble language — what does this become? It is a misdeed. If a noble one says this in the language of the border regions, and the monk does not understand the language of the border regions — what does this become? It is a misdeed. If one from the border regions says this in the language of the border regions, and the monk does not understand the language of the border regions — what does this become? It is a misdeed. If one from the border regions says this in the noble language, and the monk does not understand the noble language — what does this become? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, if a monk conveys this meaning through a bodily gesture — namely, "I will not train in this precept as the venerable one has instructed me" — what does this become? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, if a monk, perceiving one who is present alone as though he were not present alone, says, "I do not train in accordance with the words of the venerable one — train as you will" — what does this become? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, if a monk has another person say, "I will not train in this precept as the venerable one has instructed me" — what does this become? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, if a monk says on behalf of another, "The venerable one will not train in this precept as instructed" — what does this become? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, if one who has not yet received full ordination gives the instruction, and one who has not yet received full ordination says, "I will not train in this precept as the venerable one has instructed me" — what does this become? It is a misdeed. If one who has not yet received full ordination gives the instruction, and one in the act of receiving full ordination says this — what does this become? It is a misdeed. If one who has not yet received full ordination gives the instruction, and one who has fully received ordination says this — what does this become? It is a misdeed. If one in the act of receiving full ordination gives the instruction, and one in the act of receiving full ordination says this — what does this become? It is a misdeed. If one in the act of receiving full ordination gives the instruction, and one who has fully received ordination says this — what does this become? It is a misdeed. If one who has fully received ordination gives the instruction, and one who has fully received ordination says this — what does this become? It is a transgression. If one who has fully received ordination gives the instruction, and one who has not yet received full ordination says this — what does this become? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, if a layperson instructs a monk, and the monk says, "I will not train in this precept as the venerable one has instructed me" — what does this become? It is a misdeed.

Likewise, if the instruction is given by a woman, by a eunuch, by an expelled nun, by one who has slain his father or mother, by one who has killed an arhat, by one who has drawn blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent, by a non-Buddhist adherent (tīrthika), by one who has gone over to the non-Buddhists, by one who is a thief living in hiding, by one who is not residing, by one who is residing apart, by one who has previously committed an offense, or by one who has previously caused a schism — if the instruction is given by any of these and that declaration is made, all cases become misdeeds.

Venerable ones, if a monk who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, or who has sided with that schism, or monks who have given the training — if they give the instruction and that declaration is made, all cases become misdeeds.

Venerable ones, if a monk is instructed by a fully ordained nun, by a probationary nun, by a female novice,

by male novices — if the instruction is given by them and that declaration is made, all cases become misdeeds.

Venerable ones, if a monk says, "I will not train in this training as instructed by the venerable one," and his gender then changes and he becomes a nun, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, if a nun says the same, and her gender then changes and she becomes a monk, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, if a monk, perceiving someone who has received full ordination as one who has received full ordination, says, "I will not train in this training as instructed by the venerable one," what becomes of it? It is a transgression. If he perceives someone who has received full ordination as one who has not received full ordination, it becomes a misdeed. If he perceives someone who has not received full ordination as one who has received full ordination, it becomes a misdeed. If he perceives someone who has not received full ordination as one who has not received full ordination, it becomes a misdeed.

Just as a monk incurs a transgression by speaking in that way, so too does one who has given the training, and likewise a nun incurs a transgression. In the cases of a probationary nun, a female novice, and male novices, it becomes a misdeed.

In brief:
One who has gone mad, one whose mind is disturbed,
one who is ill, one who is unable to speak, one who departs —
these are the same as the fourth, namely the characteristic;
with mantra and the other, these seven,
householders and the like,
the pacification, and the nun.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable Blessed One, you have declared that if monks are quarreling and a monk is present, and he listens without speaking, he incurs a transgression. Venerable one, if monks who are mad are quarreling and a monk is present, and he listens without speaking, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed.

"Likewise, in the cases of monks whose minds are disturbed, those afflicted by illness, those who are dull-witted, those who are mute, those unable to speak, and those who have gone to dwell elsewhere — if one listens without saying anything to them, all cases become misdeeds.

"Venerable one, if monks are quarreling and a monk is present listening without speaking, and his gender then changes and he becomes a nun, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed.

"Venerable one, if a nun is present listening without speaking, and her gender then changes and she becomes a monk, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed.

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving one who has received full ordination as one who has not received full ordination, is present listening without speaking, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed.

"Venerable one, if a monk has made himself inconspicuous through mantra or medicine and is present listening without speaking, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed.

"Venerable one, if monks are quarreling and a monk causes another to listen to it, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed.

"Venerable one, if monks are quarreling and a monk listens on behalf of others, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed.

"Venerable one, if one seats a person who has not received full ordination in a place not for those who have not received full ordination, and that person listens there, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed. If one seats a person who has not received full ordination in a place for those who have received full ordination, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed. If one seats a person who has not received full ordination in a place for those who have received full ordination, and that person listens there, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed. If one seats a person who has received full ordination in a place for those who have received full ordination, and that person listens there, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed. If one seats a person who has received full ordination in a place for those who have received full ordination, and that person listens in a place for those who have received full ordination, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed. If one seats a person who has received full ordination in a place for those who have received full ordination, and that person listens in a place for those who have received full ordination, what becomes of it? It is a transgression. If one seats a person who has received full ordination in a place for those who have received full ordination, and that person listens in a place for those who have not received full ordination, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed.
